evidence: Opened all 20 blobs of the repo at main (single commit f8ff71e, 2026-09-05, 14 KB, 0 stars) via raw.githubusercontent.com, read locally: README.md (82 lines), examples/docs-topics.toml (37 lines), src/ai_docs_reviewer/{topics.py 25, coverage.py 63, judge.py 54, llm.py 51, loader.py 63, models.py 62, report.py 46, cli.py 45}, .claude/skills/docs-gap-fill/SKILL.md (14 lines), .github/workflows/docs-review.yml (34 lines), tests/test_judge_cli.py (59 lines), plus tests/test_coverage.py and tests/test_loader.py (counted, not fully read). Tree and commit list via `gh api repos/gurevich89/ai-docs-reviewer/git/trees/main?recursive=1` and `/commits`. Verified README's "15 tests" claim: `grep -hc "def test"` across the three test files sums to 15 — proven.
whatItIs: A ~400-line Python CLI (`docs-review`) plus a GitHub Actions job. The author declares the topics the docs must cover in a TOML spec (`[[topic]]` with id/title/description/keywords and optional required/min_words/max_age_days over a `[defaults]` table). The tool parses Markdown into heading-delimited sections, matches each topic by keyword, labels it covered/thin/missing, flags staleness from git commit dates, finds broken relative links, then sends only the topics that already have some coverage to an LLM that scores completeness 0-1 and lists gaps. Output is a Markdown table plus a "What to fix" work list and a JSON blob; exit 1 when a required topic is missing. A bundled Claude Code skill (`docs-gap-fill`) drafts the missing sections and must re-run the check to exit 0 before proposing. Six days old, one commit, zero stars, no eval harness — a well-built demo, not a validated tool.
measures: Document-side proxies only, and none of them validated: keyword hits per topic (coverage.py:10-18), summed word count of matched sections against a `min_words` floor (coverage.py:28-32), age of the newest matching file from `git log -1 --format=%ct` (loader.py:15-21, coverage.py:33-36), existence of relative link targets (coverage.py:41-54), and an LLM's self-reported 0-1 completeness score against a hand-written topic description (judge.py:43-50). It measures nothing about readers: no question set, no answer key, no ground truth, no comparison of the score against anything. The only scoring "evidence" in the repo is FakeLLM's arbitrary formula `score = max(0.2, 0.95 - 0.3 * len(gaps))` (llm.py:21) and a unit test asserting config scores above auth under that fake (tests/test_judge_cli.py:38).
method: Declare the answer key before looking at the text: a TOML spec lists each required topic with a natural-language `description` of what it must cover, plus per-topic thresholds inherited from a `[defaults]` table (topics.py:12-21). Run a cheap deterministic pass first — split each .md into sections by heading (fence-aware, so code blocks don't fake headings, loader.py:38-53), match a topic if its keyword appears in the heading or if two *distinct* keywords appear in the body (overlapping stems like config/configuration collapse to one, coverage.py:15-18), then label covered/thin/missing by word count and mark stale from git dates. Only then spend model calls, and only on topics the cheap pass already proved present: `if r.status == "missing": continue` (judge.py:40-41) — absence is settled by search, quality is the model's job. The judge prompt names the reader ("for a new engineer"), hands the model the topic's `description` verbatim as the rubric alongside the matched section text capped at 8000 chars with file#heading and line number attached (judge.py:10-14, 17-24, 43-44), and demands strict JSON `{score, gaps, suggestion}`; parsing is tolerant (strips fences, takes outermost braces) and any failure degrades to score=None rather than raising or silently passing (judge.py:27-34, 51-52). The report renders a status table and then a "What to fix" list where every gap is one line with its locus (report.py:23-38). The gate fails the build only on a *required* topic that is *missing*; thin is advisory unless `--fail-on-thin` (coverage.py:57-62). Repair is a separate named agent skill whose last step is to re-run the checker and confirm exit 0 before proposing the change (SKILL.md:13).

practices.practice: Spend model calls only where a cheap deterministic pass could not already settle the question. Run text search / parsing first to classify each requirement as absent-or-present; send only the present ones to the model, and let the model judge quality, never existence.
practices.locus: src/ai_docs_reviewer/judge.py:39-41 (`if r.status == "missing": continue`), gated by src/ai_docs_reviewer/coverage.py:21-38; the skip is pinned by a test asserting exactly 3 of 5 topics reach the LLM (tests/test_judge_cli.py:28-33)
practices.evidenceForIt: Argued and unit-tested for behaviour, not measured for value. No cost or accuracy numbers anywhere in the repo. The mechanism is trivially sound on cost; whether the cheap pass misclassifies (it can — see weaknesses) is untested.
practices.costAndCollision: Near-zero cost; terse's audit already pays one cheap model per question, and this would let a grep-provable miss skip the seat entirely. Collides with nothing in terse.

practices.practice: Persist the requirement set as a versioned, human-editable, diffable file that lives in the repo next to the docs, with a global defaults block and per-item overrides. Do not regenerate the checklist from scratch on every run.
practices.locus: examples/docs-topics.toml:1-37 ([defaults] at 1-4; per-topic override `min_words = 80` at 29 and `required = false` at 36); merge logic at src/ai_docs_reviewer/topics.py:18-20
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. README.md:8-9 states the goal ('becomes a CI check ... instead of a question nobody answers') with no data behind it. The defaults-plus-override merge is real code, not prose.
practices.costAndCollision: Adds one artifact per audited repo. For terse this is the strongest borrow: the audit's answer key is derived fresh from code each run, so two runs are not comparable and a regression is invisible. Writing the question set to a file makes the audit diffable. Cost: the file goes stale against the code, which is the exact failure terse exists to catch — so it must be regenerable from code and diffed, not hand-maintained.

practices.practice: Put the reader in the judging prompt, hand the judge the requirement text verbatim as its rubric, and make the judge return structured JSON with a score, a short gap list and one suggestion — not prose.
practices.locus: src/ai_docs_reviewer/judge.py:10-14 (SYSTEM names 'a new engineer' and pins the JSON shape) and 43-44 (the topic's own `description` is pasted in as 'What it must cover')
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. No ablation, no comparison against an unprompted judge. Note terse's own 2026-09-10 bake-off found published standards lose to unguided controls, so a prompt-level reader profile is the part with independent support here, not the rubric.
practices.costAndCollision: Free. terse's revise pass 1 already builds a reader profile; this says to carry that profile into the *judging* prompt too, not just the writing prompt. No collision.

practices.practice: Make unparseable or malformed model output degrade to 'no verdict', never to a pass and never to a crash. Strip code fences, take the outermost braces, and on failure record the raw text as a note with the score set to null.
practices.locus: src/ai_docs_reviewer/judge.py:27-34 (`_extract_json`) and 51-52 (`except ... : r.llm_score, r.llm_gaps, r.llm_suggestion = None, [], raw[:200]`); pinned by tests/test_judge_cli.py:40-42
practices.evidenceForIt: Argued and unit-tested (a 'garbage' reply leaves every score None). Not measured against real model output rates.
practices.costAndCollision: Free, ~10 lines. terse's audit scores right/wrong answers across many seats; a malformed seat reply silently counted as wrong would inflate the failure count and mislabel the failure class. Worth adopting as a fourth outcome alongside lie/placement/findability.

practices.practice: Derive document freshness from `git log -1 --format=%ct -- <path>`, falling back to filesystem mtime, and set `fetch-depth: 0` in CI. A fresh checkout gives every file the same mtime, so mtime-based staleness is meaningless in CI.
practices.locus: src/ai_docs_reviewer/loader.py:15-21 and 54 (`mtime = _git_mtime(path) or path.stat().st_mtime`); .github/workflows/docs-review.yml:23 (`fetch-depth: 0 # full history so freshness uses git dates`)
practices.evidenceForIt: Argued, and the reasoning is verifiable from how actions/checkout works — the comment on workflow line 23 states the mechanism. Not measured.
practices.costAndCollision: ~8 lines plus one CI setting. Only relevant if terse ever reports staleness; it does not today. Cheap to keep in the library as an operational footnote.

practices.practice: End the repair pass by re-running the measurement and requiring the gate to go green before the change is proposed to the human. The repair is not finished when the text is written; it is finished when the number moves.
practices.locus: .claude/skills/docs-gap-fill/SKILL.md:13 ('Re-run the reviewer and confirm exit code 0 before proposing the change'); the whole skill is 5 numbered steps at SKILL.md:8-13
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted, and the skill has clearly never been run against anything (repo is 6 days old with one commit and no example output). The idea is nonetheless the same loop terse already proved once: the 3-right → 6-right result on 2026-09-10 came from re-measuring after repair.
practices.costAndCollision: One extra audit run per revise cycle — real token cost, and it doubles the cheap-model spend. Given the owner's 2026-09-07 objection to large fan-outs, make re-measurement re-ask only the questions that failed, not the whole set.

practices.practice: Render the audit as a work list, not a grade: one section per failing item, each gap on its own line with its file#heading and line number, and the expected content restated from the spec when the item is missing entirely.
practices.locus: src/ai_docs_reviewer/report.py:23-38 ('## What to fix'); loci are attached upstream at src/ai_docs_reviewer/judge.py:23 (`f"### {key} (line {s.line})"`) and coverage.py:37
practices.evidenceForIt: Asserted. No reader study on the report format. The summary table at report.py:14-22 is the conventional part; the 'What to fix' list is the useful part.
practices.costAndCollision: Free. terse's audit already classifies failures as lie/placement/findability; this adds 'and say which file and line, and restate what was expected'. No collision.

weaknesses:
Three anti-patterns to record, none of which should reach terse's library as a recommendation.

(1) `min_words` as a completeness proxy. `Topic.min_words` defaults to 60 (models.py:35), the example raises troubleshooting to 80 (docs-topics.toml:29), and coverage.py:28-32 labels a topic "thin" purely on the summed word count of matched sections. This rewards padding and is the same family the owner already rejected on evidence (hard word limits). It is also self-defeating here: adding filler words to an existing section flips thin→covered without changing what a reader learns.

(2) Keyword-hit coverage. `_section_matches` (coverage.py:10-18) does substring matching — a heading containing any keyword, or a body containing two "distinct" keywords, where distinctness is decided by one substring test. The README concedes the failure itself at lines 75-77: a short keyword like `env` also matches "environment" and over-reports coverage. So the pre-filter that decides which topics reach the model is a substring grep, which means a topic can be judged "covered" by a passing mention and never sent to the judge as missing — and, worse, a topic genuinely documented under different words is declared missing and fails the build. There is no test for a false positive or false negative on real prose.

(3) The CI gate on a fixed declared topic list (coverage.py:57-62, workflow lines 27-31). Exit 1 when a required topic is absent is a structure mandate by another name — adjacent to the already-rejected "Diataxis as a required pass". The topic list is hand-written by whoever set it up, so the gate enforces one person's idea of what documentation must contain, permanently, with no feedback from readers.

Evidence quality overall: nothing in this repo is measured. Created 2026-09-05, one commit, 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 issues. The 15 tests (README.md:49 — verified by count, proven) are unit tests that run offline against `FakeLLM`, whose entire scoring model is `score = max(0.2, 0.95 - 0.3 * len(gaps))` with gaps triggered by whether the string "example" or a code fence appears (llm.py:13-23). No ablation, no ground truth, no comparison to a human reviewer, no record of the tool ever being pointed at a real docs tree other than the 2-file `examples/docs` fixture that was authored to produce one of each status (README.md:40). Treat every practice above as a design idea from a careful engineer, not as a validated finding. One minor robustness bug worth noting if any of this is ported: `_git_mtime` runs git with `cwd=path.parent` and passes an absolute path (loader.py:17-18), so it works, but it spawns one subprocess per .md file with a 5s timeout each — on a large docs tree that is the slowest part of the deterministic pass.
